nodes.label: Moby-Dick
nodes.note:
Herman Melville, 1851. A sailor called Ishmael tells the story of the whaling ship Pequod and its captain, Ahab, who is set on killing the white whale that took his leg.

Tap a branch to unfold it.

nodes.label: Story arc
nodes.note: The plot is simple: sign on, sail, hunt, sink. Melville stretches it over 135 chapters, with long detours into whales and whaling between the main events.

nodes.label: Ishmael goes to sea
nodes.note: Restless and gloomy, with a “damp, drizzly November” in his soul, Ishmael decides to sign on as a common sailor on a whaling voyage.

nodes.label: A bed shared with Queequeg
nodes.note: In New Bedford the inn is full, so Ishmael shares a bed with a tattooed South Sea harpooneer. He is terrified at first. By morning they are friends.

nodes.label: Ahab's oath
nodes.note: Ahab gathers the crew on the quarter-deck, nails a gold coin to the mast, and makes them swear to hunt Moby Dick. The voyage stops being a business trip and becomes a revenge mission.

nodes.label: The three-day chase
nodes.note: Moby Dick is finally sighted. Over three days the whale wrecks the boats, then rams and sinks the Pequod. Ahab is caught by his own harpoon line and pulled under.

nodes.label: Ishmael alone survives
nodes.note: In the short epilogue, Ishmael floats for a day and a night on Queequeg's coffin until the ship Rachel, still searching for its own lost crew, picks him up.

nodes.label: Characters
nodes.note: A small cast on a crowded ship. Ishmael narrates, Ahab drives the story, and the white whale is barely seen until the end.

nodes.label: Ishmael
nodes.note: The narrator. A curious, funny, open-minded schoolteacher turned sailor. He often disappears from his own story and becomes a voice thinking about whales, work and meaning.

nodes.label: Captain Ahab
nodes.note: Captain of the Pequod. He walks on an ivory leg made from a whale's jaw. Losing his leg to Moby Dick has hardened into monomania: he reads the whale as the face of everything that has wronged him.

nodes.label: Queequeg
nodes.note: A harpooneer and the son of a Pacific island king. Calm, generous and brave, he saves a man who mocked him from drowning. He becomes Ishmael's closest friend.

nodes.label: Starbuck
nodes.note: The first mate, a careful Quaker from Nantucket. He sees that Ahab's hunt will doom the crew and argues against it, but he never manages to stop him.
nodes.quote: Vengeance on a dumb brute! that simply smote thee from blindest instinct!

nodes.label: Moby Dick
nodes.note: A huge, unusually white sperm whale, known to sailors for wrecking boats. Whether it is a dumb animal or a symbol of something larger is the book's central question.

nodes.label: Themes
nodes.note: The big ideas the novel keeps returning to.

nodes.label: Obsession
nodes.note: Ahab's single-mindedness gives him great force. It also pulls a whole crew into his private war. The book asks what happens when one person's fixation becomes everyone's job.

nodes.label: Fate vs free will
nodes.note: Prophecies and omens pile up as the ship nears the whale. Ahab claims his path is fixed (“This whole act's immutably decreed”), yet he keeps choosing it, again and again.

nodes.label: Limits of knowledge
nodes.note: Ishmael measures, classifies and dissects the whale, and still admits he cannot really know it. The harder he looks, the less certain he becomes.
nodes.quote: Dissect him how I may, then, I but go skin deep; I know him not, and never will.

nodes.label: Friendship across cultures
nodes.note: Ishmael and Queequeg's friendship cuts across race, religion and language. Ishmael's quick shift from fear to affection is one of the warmest parts of the book.
nodes.quote: Better sleep with a sober cannibal than a drunken Christian.

nodes.label: Key ideas
nodes.note: Points worth remembering about how the book works.

nodes.label: Cetology chapters
nodes.note: Melville breaks off the story for chapters of cetology, whaling technique and history. These digressions aren't filler. They show Ishmael trying to master the whale with facts.

nodes.label: One coin, many readings
nodes.note: Each crew member studies the gold doubloon on the mast and sees himself in it. This is a small model of the whole novel: meaning depends on who is looking.

nodes.label: The Whiteness of the Whale
nodes.note: A whole chapter on why whiteness frightens. It can stand for purity, but also for blankness, a colour that is “the visible absence of colour”. It explains why this whale haunts the crew.

nodes.label: Places
nodes.note: Where the story happens: a whaling coast, then one ship on the open ocean.

nodes.label: The Pequod
nodes.note: An old Nantucket whaler named after a Native American tribe that had been wiped out, which is already a grim sign. At sea it meets other ships for a gam, and each meeting brings news of the white whale.

nodes.label: New Bedford & Nantucket
nodes.note: The whaling towns of Massachusetts. In New Bedford Ishmael hears Father Mapple's sermon on Jonah. On Nantucket he and Queequeg sign on to the Pequod.

nodes.label: Quotes
nodes.note: Lines worth knowing by heart.

nodes.label: “Call me Ishmael.”
nodes.note: One of the most famous opening lines in English. It is friendly and informal, and it hints that “Ishmael” may not be his real name.

nodes.label: “Pasteboard masks”
nodes.note: Ahab explains to Starbuck why he hunts: the visible world is a mask, and he means to strike through it at whatever is behind.
nodes.quote: All visible objects, man, are but as pasteboard masks. … If man will strike, strike through the mask!

nodes.label: “To the last I grapple”
nodes.note: Ahab's last words as he throws his final harpoon.
nodes.quote: To the last I grapple with thee; from hell's heart I stab at thee; for hate's sake I spit my last breath at thee.
